nameStory: Corn gromwell gets its name from its habit of growing in agricultural fields, especially corn crops, where it often appears as a weedy companion. The word 'gromwell' comes from an old French term meaning 'grain of the sun,' referring to the hard, bead-like seeds that were once thought to resemble tiny pearls or grains.
description: Corn gromwell is a rough, hairy annual plant that typically grows 6-18 inches tall with a somewhat sprawling habit. It produces small, inconspicuous white or pale blue flowers along its branching stems throughout the growing season. The entire plant has a coarse, sandpapery texture due to stiff hairs covering the stems and leaves. As a member of the borage family, it shares characteristics with plants like forget-me-nots and comfrey, though it's much less showy than its relatives.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves that feel remarkably rough and sandpapery when you run your finger along them - almost like fine grit sandpaper due to tiny stiff hairs

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white or very pale blue flowers, only about 1/8 inch across, that appear in clusters along the upper stems - easily overlooked due to their small size

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Hard, smooth, pearl-like seeds that are pale gray to white and feel like tiny pebbles when rolled between your fingers

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, somewhat sprawling annual with multiple branching stems that create a bushy appearance, rarely growing taller than knee-high

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Rough, hairy stems that feel bristly to the touch and often have a reddish tinge, especially near the base

habitat: Corn gromwell thrives in disturbed soils, particularly agricultural fields, roadsides, and waste areas where the ground has been tilled or otherwise disrupted. It prefers well-drained, sandy or gravelly soils and is most commonly found in areas with full sun exposure. In New England, look for it in farm fields, along field edges, and in abandoned lots.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes with distinctively rough, sandpapery leaves that are already noticeably bristly to the touch.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full size and produce their tiny white flowers continuously through the warm months, with the rough texture of leaves becoming even more pronounced.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue blooming until frost, and the characteristic hard, bead-like seeds become most noticeable as they ripen to a pale gray color.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die back completely, leaving only the hard seeds to overwinter in the soil and germinate the following spring.

funFact: The seeds of corn gromwell are so hard and stone-like that they can remain viable in soil for decades - some have been known to germinate after being buried for over 30 years, earning it the alternate name 'stone seed'!
confusionNotes: Corn gromwell might be confused with other small-flowered weedy plants, but the distinctive sandpaper-rough texture of its leaves is unique - if it doesn't feel like you're touching fine grit sandpaper, it's probably not corn gromwell.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'corn gromwell,' this plant isn't related to corn at all - the name simply refers to its tendency to grow in cornfields. It's actually a European native that arrived in North America as an agricultural weed, likely mixed in with crop seeds.
compareHints: Since corn gromwell is the only Buglossoides species commonly found in New England, compare it to other borage family members like forget-me-nots and viper's bugloss. Unlike forget-me-nots with their sky-blue flowers and softer leaves, corn gromwell has tiny, pale flowers and extremely rough, sandpapery foliage. Viper's bugloss is much taller with bright blue flowers and less uniformly rough leaves.
